\begin{bankq}[id=SI03-P1-PHY-S3-Q01, source={Score-I - Test 03 (07 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Variable mass}, answer={2.85 to 2.86}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: speed, a raindrop gaining mass while falling through mist | steps: dp/dt = m g with variable mass m = k r^3; dm/dt = rho_mist pi r^2 v; solve constant acceleration g/7; compute asked | I: variable mass system with accretion}]

\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SI09-P2-PHY-S3-G3-4, source={Score-I - Test 09 (16 Feb 2022)}, questions={3-4}]
A pendulum consists of a bob of mass $m=0.1$ kg and a massless inextensible string of length $L=1.0$ m. It is suspended from a fixed point at height $H=0.9$ m above a frictionless horizontal floor. Initially, the bob of the pendulum is lying on the floor at rest vertically below the point of suspension. A horizontal impulse $P=0.2$ kg-m/s is imparted to the bob at some instant. After the bob slides for some distance, the string becomes taut and the bob lifts off the floor. The magnitude of the angular momentum of the pendulum about the point of suspension just before the bob lifts off is $J$ kg-m$^2$/s. The kinetic energy of the pendulum just after the lift-off is $K$ Joules.
\end{bankpassage}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI17-P2-PHY-S2-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 17 (17 Apr 2022)}, paper=2, qno=4, type=numerical, subtopic={Momentum}, answer={112.5}, answer_src=solved, working={At the top the total vertical momentum is zero: u\_A + 2u = 0 so u\_A = -2u. The printed key has no row for this decimal-answer section.}, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: height at which a projectile explodes into three equal fragments | steps: horizontal explosion at top conserves vertical momentum zero; vertical velocities of the three fragments; kinematics with landing times 3 s and 6 s; solve for height}]

\end{bankq}

\textbf{Thrust on a Rocket \& Bernoulli's equation.}

Thrust is the force which moves the rocket through the air and through space. Thrust is generated by the propulsion system. An engine does work on a gas or liquid, called a working fluid. Consider a chamber of cross-sectional area A filled with a gas of density $\rho$ at a pressure P as shown in figure. Let there be a small orifice of cross-sectional area A$_0$ at the bottom of the chamber. The speed $v_0$ with which the gas escape through the orifice can be found using Bernouli's equation as
$$P-P_0=\dfrac12\rho\left(v_0^2-v^2\right)$$
Where P$_0$ represents atmospheric pressure just outside the orifice, v is the speed of the following gas inside the chamber and $v_0$ is the speed of gas through orifice. Since the gas density is negligible, pressure variation with height in the chamber can be neglected. (A $\gg$ A$_0$) (Use P = $10\times10^5$ Pa, P$_0$ = $1\times10^5$ Pa, $\rho$ = $0.5\times10^3$ kg/m$^3$, A$_0$ = 0.5 m$^2$)

\par
\bfig{120}{SII37_p1phy_n12_rocket.png}\par
\end{bankpassage}

When the relative velocity of approach increases to 3 m/sec, the velocity of the centre of mass decreases to 0.25 m/sec\\
\textbf{Statement-II :-} The total kinetic energy as seen from ground is $\dfrac12\mu V_{\text{rel}}^2+\dfrac12MV_{\text{c.m}}^2$ and here $\mu$ is reduced mass $\mu=\dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$ and $M$ is total mass $M=(m_1+m_2)$ and in absence of external force, total mechanical energy remains conserved

\opt{A}{Statement-I is true, Statement-II is true}
\opt{B}{Statement-I is false, Statement-II is true}
\opt{C}{Statement-I is false, Statement-II is false}
\opt{D}{Statement-I is true, Statement-II is false}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Two particles, 1 and 2, each of mass \textit m, are connected by a massless spring, and are on a horizontal frictionless plane, as shown in the figure. Initially, the two particles, with their center of mass at \textit x$_0$, are oscillating with amplitude \textit a and angular frequency $\omega$. Thus, their positions at time \textit t are given by\par
\textit x$_1$(\textit t) = (\textit x$_0$ + \textit d) + \textit a sin $\omega t$ and \textit x$_2$(\textit t) = (\textit x$_0$ $-$ \textit d) $-$ \textit a sin $\omega t$, respectively, where \textit d $>$ 2\textit a. Particle 3 of mass \textit m moves towards this system with speed \textit u$_0$ = \textit a$\omega$/2, and undergoes instantaneous elastic collision with particle 2, at time \textit t$_0$. Finally, particles 1 and 2 acquire a center of mass speed v$_\mathrm{cm}$ and oscillate with amplitude \textit b and the same angular frequency $\omega$.\par
\bfig{172.4}{SA38_p2_phy_s3_para3_4_1.png}
